title: Three Indians Storm US Open Badminton Semifinals as Srikanth, Teen Prodigy Rounak, and Devika Sihag Shine in California
excerpt: Former world No. 1 Kidambi Srikanth leads a three-strong Indian charge into the last four at Fullerton, joined by 18-year-old qualifier Rounak Chouhan and Thailand Masters champion Devika Sihag
body:
In what is shaping up to be one of Indian badminton's finest weeks on American soil, three shuttlers have powered their way into the semifinals of the Yonex US Open Super 300 in Fullerton, California — a result that has the sport's diaspora community buzzing with excitement ahead of a blockbuster Saturday.

Kidambi Srikanth, the former world No. 1 and 2021 World Championship silver medallist, led the charge with a commanding quarterfinal victory over Chinese Taipei's Liao Jhuo-Fu. After a blistering opening game (21-9), Srikanth weathered a second-game wobble (12-21) before reasserting control in the decider, winning 21-8 to book his place in the last four.

Now ranked 38th in the world, the 33-year-old from Ravulapalem, Andhra Pradesh, is showing signs of the form that once carried him to four Superseries titles in a single year. A graduate of Pullela Gopichand's celebrated academy in Hyderabad, Srikanth's career has traced the arc of Indian badminton's broader rise — from his world No. 1 ranking in April 2018, through a Thomas Cup gold medal in 2022, a bronze at the 2026 edition, and a silver at the 2021 World Championships. He faces fourth-seeded Brazilian Yudi Okimoto in Saturday's semifinal.

![World Championship — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/22/Memorial_Luiz_C%C3%A1ssio_dos_Santos_Werneck_27.jpg)

A teenager's fairy tale continues

> "The 18-year-old from Madhya Pradesh, who entered the tournament as a qualifier with no ranking to speak of at this level, followed up his stunning second-round upset of world No."

If Srikanth's run is a story of veteran resilience, Rounak Chouhan's is a fairy tale unfolding in real time. The 18-year-old from Madhya Pradesh, who entered the tournament as a qualifier with no ranking to speak of at this level, followed up his stunning second-round upset of world No. 6 Chou Tien Chen — a result that sent shockwaves through the badminton world earlier this week — with another quarterfinal win, this time defeating Israel's Misha Zilberman 23-21, 21-11.

![Andhra Pradesh — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Tirumala_090615.jpg/3840px-Tirumala_090615.jpg)

Rounak is now in his first-ever BWF Super 300 semifinal, a remarkable achievement for a teenager who was grinding through qualifying rounds just days ago. His trajectory mirrors the kind of breakthrough stories Indian badminton has produced with increasing regularity in recent years, from Lakshya Sen's early emergence to Saina Nehwal's pioneering run over a decade ago. He faces eighth-seeded Su Li Yang of Chinese Taipei on Saturday, carrying the hopes of a nation that has grown accustomed to expecting the unexpected from its youngest talent.

Devika Sihag adds women's singles firepower

Completing the Indian trifecta is Devika Sihag, who produced a gutsy performance to knock out third-seeded Japanese shuttler Riko Gunji. The Thailand Masters champion needed every ounce of composure in a tight two-game battle, edging past Gunji 22-20, 21-19 in a match that could have gone either way on its razor-thin margins.

![Pullela Gopichand — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/03/Pullela_Gopichand_2016_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Devika's semifinal opponent is second-seeded Line Christophersen of Denmark — the same player who ended compatriot Tanvi Sharma's run in the quarterfinals (21-16, 11-21, 21-11). Rakshitha Ramraj's tournament also ended at the last-eight stage, falling to Canada's Rachel Chan 21-15, 16-21, 12-21 in a hard-fought contest.

In mixed doubles, seventh-seeded pair Dhruv Rawat and K Maneesha had earlier advanced through the draw, adding further Indian representation across categories at the tournament.

A diaspora moment in Southern California

The timing and setting could not be more fitting. Fullerton sits at the heart of Southern California's sprawling Indian-American community — one of the largest and most active in the United States. Orange County alone is home to tens of thousands of Indian-origin families, many of whom have historically found badminton courts a gathering place for community, recreation, and cultural identity.

With three Indians in the semifinals and the tantalising possibility of an all-Indian men's singles final on Sunday — should both Srikanth and the teenage Rounak prevail in their respective matches — the weekend promises to be a celebration of Indian badminton on diaspora turf. For the NRI community that has long championed the sport in recreation centres, temples, and community halls across cities like Los Angeles, San Jose, and Houston, seeing their country's shuttlers dominate a BWF event in their own backyard is a moment to savour.

The atmosphere at the Titan Gym is expected to be electric. The semifinals are scheduled for Saturday, June 28, with finals on Sunday.
